Hadoram
huh-DOH-ram
proper noun
Hebrew Hadoram (H1913), commonly read Hadar is exalted, the first element being the name of a Syrian deity; the man who served Rehoboam is called Adoram in Kings and Adoniram in the record of Solomon's levy.

Biblical Definition

Three men bear this name. The first is a son of Joktan in the table of nations, one of the Arabian peoples descended from Shem (Gen 10:27; 1Ch 1:21). The second is a son of Tou king of Hamath, sent to David with vessels of gold and silver and brass to congratulate him on defeating Hadarezer, the common enemy of both (1Ch 18:10). The third is the officer who was over the tribute under Rehoboam, called Adoram in Kings, and his end is one of the sharpest scenes in the history of the divided kingdom. Rehoboam, having answered Israel's plea for a lighter yoke with a threat of scorpions, sent the tax collector to enforce it, and all Israel stoned him with stones, that he died. Therefore king Rehoboam made speed to get him up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem (1Ki 12:18). The man had served Solomon over the levy and Rehoboam over the tribute, and the king sent him into a city that had just renounced the crown. He was stoned for a policy he did not make, by people whose complaint was just, at the order of a king who then ran.

Origin & Era

The name of three men: a son of Joktan, a son of Tou king of Hamath, and Rehoboam's officer over the tribute, who was stoned by Israel.

HADORAM, Hebrew Hadoram, commonly read Hadar is exalted.

1. A son of Joktan in the table of the nations, of the sons of Shem.

2. A son of Tou king of Hamath, sent with gifts to congratulate David.

3. The officer over the tribute under Rehoboam; called Adoram in the book of Kings.

All Israel stoned him with stones, and Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem in his chariot.

Key Scripture

Gen 10:27 — "And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah,"

1Ch 1:21 — "Hadoram also, and Uzal, and Diklah,"

1Ki 12:18 — "Then king Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute; and all Israel stoned him with stones, that he died. Therefore king Rehoboam made speed to get him up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem."

2Sa 20:24 — "And Adoram was over the tribute: and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder:"

Modern Corruption

Leaders are judged by their intentions and their subordinates by their outcomes; Scripture puts the cost of Rehoboam's folly on the man he sent.

expand to see more

The stoning of Adoram is the bill for Rehoboam's speech. The old men had counselled the king to speak good words to the people and they would be his servants for ever; the young men who had grown up with him advised the threat of scorpions; he took the second counsel, the ten tribes departed, and then he sent the tax officer into the breach. The man who died was the man who had been doing that job since Solomon's day. Rehoboam kept his chariot.

Scripture is unsentimental about the weight of office. My brethren, be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation (Jas 3:1); the shepherd who flees when he sees the wolf coming is named a hireling because the sheep are not his (Joh 10:12-13); and the Good Shepherd is known by the opposite motion — He giveth His life for the sheep. The principle to recover is that authority is measured by who absorbs the cost when a decision goes wrong. A leader whose errors are paid for by the people under him has not led them; he has spent them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Hadoram (H1913); the same officer appears as Adoram (H151) and Adoniram (H141), my lord is exalted.

expand to see more

Hebrew Hadoram (H1913) — a son of Joktan (Gen 10:27), a son of Tou (1Ch 18:10), and Rehoboam's officer (2Ch 10:18).

Hebrew Adoram (H151) — the form used in 2 Samuel 20:24 and 1 Kings 12:18 for the officer over the tribute.

Hebrew mas (H4522) — tribute, forced labour, a levy; the burden Israel asked Rehoboam to lighten.

Hebrew ol (H5923) — a yoke; thy father made our yoke grievous (1Ki 12:4).

Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hireling; the hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling (Joh 10:13).

Usage

"“And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah” — among the sons of Joktan."

"“Then king Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute”."

"“King Rehoboam made speed to get him up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem”."
